claims.text: The initial lightweight Mg-containing high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
Elevated-temperature annealing causes the metastable solid solution to decompose partially.
The decomposition proceeds through a nucleation-and-growth pathway.
Decomposition produces finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Thermodynamic driving forces promote phase separation from the metastable state.
Mg diffusion accelerates local chemical ordering.
Annealing temperature influences the characteristic length scale of phase decomposition.
A fine dispersion of intermetallic precipitates improves formation or integrity of protective oxide layers.
Continued thermal exposure causes the precipitates to grow and coarsen.
Coarsened Mg-rich precipitates accumulate and become interconnected along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary accumulation of precipitates creates discontinuities in protective corrosion or oxide films.
Protective-film discontinuities increase susceptibility to corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Samples retaining fine, dispersed precipitates will have superior corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast metastable state.
Samples with coarsened, interconnected grain-boundary precipitates will have degraded corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Temperatures of approximately 850–1050 °C are within the relevant high-temperature oxidation service regime and are sufficient to drive phase separation.
The proposed pathway applies below temperatures causing complete homogenization or melting and over durations sufficient for precipitation and coarsening.
